slides.title: Brain activity produces perception and action
body: **Behavioral neuroscience** studies how the nervous system produces perception, movement, memory, and emotion. A **neuron** is a nerve cell. Neurons receive signals, change their electrical activity, and send signals to other cells.
Sensory systems detect events outside and inside the body. Motor systems organize actions such as reaching, walking, or speaking. Memory allows an earlier experience to change a later response.
An experiment can measure both the action and the activity of the cells involved. The scientist asks what the animal does, which cells are active, and how changing those cells changes the action.

slides.title: Generalization identifies recurring behavioral rules
body: **Generalization** identifies a rule that applies to several observations. Comparing the same behavior in different situations reveals which conditions reliably change it.
A mouse may build a nest when its surroundings are cold. Pregnancy can also increase nest building, even when cold is not the immediate trigger.

The movements are similar, but the conditions that start them differ. Describing those conditions gives a behavioral rule. Investigating the signals that trigger the movements explains how the rule arises.

slides.title: Goldfish drive toward a terrestrial visual target
body: Givon and colleagues placed a goldfish tank on a wheeled platform. The **fish-operated vehicle**, or FOV, moved according to the fish’s location and the direction it faced.
A pink board marked the destination in a 3 × 4 metre room. Reaching it produced a food pellet. The goldfish remained in water while its swimming actions moved the tank across the floor.
With training, arrivals became more frequent and routes more direct. The fish learned to use an unfamiliar movement system to approach a visual goal outside its tank.

slides.title: Fish position determines vehicle movement
body: A camera above the tank measured the goldfish’s position and orientation. Software identified its body outline and estimated the direction it faced.
Near a tank boundary, facing outward could command the wheels to move. Swimming to a new location inside the tank therefore changed the platform’s direction through the room.

The researchers recorded both fish position and vehicle position. The first measured the controlling action; the second measured the resulting route. These records made changes during training measurable.

slides.title: Orientation and tank position control the wheels
body: The vehicle moved when the fish approached a boundary and faced outward. Facing inward or staying near the tank center could leave the platform stationary.
Wheel movement developed over about one second after a command. The fish therefore experienced a delay between changing position and seeing the tank move through the room.
A laser-ranging system prevented movement within 20 centimetres of an obstacle. The fish’s actions, the mechanical delay, and automatic collision prevention all shaped the routes available.

slides.title: Rewarded training produces more direct routes
body: **Operant learning** changes behavior through its consequences. In the vehicle task, arrival at the pink board produced food. The fish could try again after the tank returned to the start.
Early routes wandered and often missed the target. Later routes became more direct, with more successful arrivals and shorter journeys.
Reward followed successful control of the vehicle. Across repeated attempts, the fish changed its movements so the tank reached the goal more efficiently.

slides.title: Changed starting positions test route flexibility
body: Givon and colleagues changed where the vehicle started. The visual target remained the destination, but the fish needed a different route to reach it.
Fish could approach the target from these new starting positions. Their actions were therefore not confined to repeating one trained path through the room.
A visible goal can guide movement when the starting point changes. The fish must select movements using its current position rather than only reproduce a fixed sequence.

slides.title: Decoys and target relocation test visual guidance
body: The researchers added visual decoys and relocated the target. These changes tested which visual information guided the vehicle’s movement.
Fish continued to approach the rewarded target under changed conditions. The experiments varied objects in the room while recording where the vehicle went.
Navigation required detecting the destination and choosing actions that moved the tank toward it. Changes in the scene revealed how the fish used external visual information during the task.

slides.title: Reduction explains behavior through its parts
body: **Reduction** explains a complex event through its component processes. Nest building can be examined as sensory detection, internal signals, and movements that carry material into a nest.
Temperature-sensitive systems detect cooling. Pregnancy alters **hormones**, chemical messengers released within the body. These signals act on neural systems that organize the animal’s movements.

Neurons also need a stable chemical environment. **Astrocytes**, star-shaped supporting cells, help regulate this environment and supply metabolic support. Explaining a behavior can therefore involve both neurons and the cells maintaining them.

slides.title: Behavior has a function and a biological mechanism
body: A behavior’s **function** describes what it accomplishes. A nest helps maintain body temperature and shelters offspring. Its **mechanism** describes the processes that produce the construction movements.
Sensory signals, hormones, and motor circuits determine when the animal gathers material and where it places it. The completed nest then changes the animal’s surroundings.

The barreleye fish provides a sensory example. Its transparent head region and conspicuous eyes are visible in the footage. Studying an eye’s structure asks how it gathers information; studying its use asks how that information guides behavior.

slides.title: Brain and body systems coordinate perception and action
body: The **central nervous system** consists of the brain and spinal cord. **Peripheral nerves** carry information between this central system and the body. Sensory information enters through nerves, and motor commands return to muscles.

The **cerebral cortex** is the outer sheet of the cerebrum. Different cortical regions contribute to vision, movement, and language. These regions exchange signals as a person sees an object and reaches for it.

Brain damage can interrupt a particular step in this process. A person may still see an object but have difficulty naming it or moving toward it. The affected behavior helps identify which brain functions have changed.

slides.title: Anatomical observations localized speech-related function
body: Paul Broca examined a person who had lost much of his ability to produce speech. After death, the brain contained damage in the left frontal region.

**Localization of function** means that particular regions make particular contributions to behavior. **Broca’s area** participates in processes needed for producing speech. Damage can interfere with converting intended words into spoken output.
Language also requires other regions for hearing, recognizing words, and retrieving information. Speaking depends on signals passing among these systems, not only on the activity of one location.

slides.title: Staining revealed the cellular organization of the brain
body: A stain makes selected structures visible under a microscope. The **Golgi method** colors a small fraction of neurons, revealing their cell bodies and branching processes.

Santiago Ramón y Cajal examined these stained cells. He described neurons as distinct cells whose processes approach other cells. This cellular organization became central to explanations of neural signaling.

**Dendrites** receive many incoming signals. An **axon** carries outgoing electrical signals toward terminals. The labeled neuron image identifies these structures, which perform different steps in communication.

slides.title: Abnormal neural activity and recovery reveal plasticity
body: A **seizure** is a period of abnormal neural activity that can disrupt sensation, movement, or awareness. Rasmussen encephalitis causes brain inflammation and can produce repeated seizures in one cerebral hemisphere.

A **hemisphere** is one of the cerebrum’s two large sides. In severe childhood cases, disconnecting the affected side can reduce seizures. **Plasticity** allows remaining circuits to change as the child develops and practices skills.

Dogra and colleagues recorded a zebrafish epilepsy model using a fluorescent calcium indicator. Bright changes mark calcium events in brain cells. The fish carries altered citrate-transport genes; its neural activity provides an experimental example of abnormal excitability.

slides.title: A single hemisphere retains organized brain networks
body: Kliemann and colleagues studied adults who had undergone **hemispherectomy**, removal or disconnection of one cerebral hemisphere, during childhood. Structural magnetic resonance imaging, or **MRI**, documented the remaining brain tissue.
The adults retained recognizable networks for vision, movement, attention, and other functions. A **brain network** is a set of regions whose activity is organized together.
The remaining hemisphere contained several distinct systems. Childhood brain reorganization preserved this division of work while changing how strongly different systems interacted.

slides.title: Brain activity can be measured through its blood supply
body: Active brain tissue needs oxygen and nutrients. Local blood flow changes with neural activity. **Functional MRI**, or fMRI, measures a signal related to blood oxygenation across brain regions.

**Functional connectivity** describes how closely two regions’ signals fluctuate together. Similar rises and falls indicate coordinated activity over the measured period. Researchers compare many regions to identify networks.

Visual, movement-related, and attention-related areas form distinguishable groups. Comparing their fluctuations reveals how activity is organized within a hemisphere, including after childhood surgery.

slides.title: Different brain networks interact more strongly after surgery
body: Kliemann and colleagues compared activity within a network with activity between different networks. Adults with childhood hemispherectomy retained strong coordination within their remaining brain networks.

Different networks also fluctuated together more strongly than in most participants with two hemispheres. Visual, motor, and attention-related systems remained distinguishable but interacted more extensively.

The authors proposed that greater interaction among networks helps describe the brain’s reorganization after early surgery. The remaining tissue maintains several kinds of function within one hemisphere.

slides.title: Biological explanations replaced early heart-centered ideas
body: Hippocrates associated thought and emotion with the brain. Aristotle assigned a major role to the heart and described the brain as a cooling organ. These accounts placed mental functions in different organs.

Galen examined nervous systems in several animals. Nerves ran between sense organs, muscles, and the brain. Their paths made a brain-centered explanation of sensation and action anatomically plausible.
Later investigators tested the effects of damaged nerves and brain tissue. A change in sensation or movement after damage helped identify the structure’s contribution to behavior.

slides.title: Monism treats mental activity as brain function
body: **Dualism** treats mind and body as different kinds of entities. **Monism**, in a biological account, treats mental activity as a function of the physical brain.

Descartes proposed mechanical explanations for some nervous-system responses. He also proposed that a nonphysical mind interacted with the body through the pineal gland. This was a historical proposal about mental activity.

Neuroscience measures physical events during perception, memory, and action. It also changes a biological process and measures the resulting behavior. These experiments examine how mental functions arise from the nervous system.

slides.title: Selection changes inherited traits across generations
body: **Natural selection** changes inherited traits across generations. When a heritable trait affects survival or reproduction, individuals carrying it may leave different numbers of offspring.
The next generation then contains a different distribution of traits. Selection acts on existing variation; individual animals do not acquire a useful inherited trait because they need it.

The dragonfish footage provides a visible example of unusual body and light-producing structures. Explaining their evolution requires evidence about inheritance and reproductive consequences. Their appearance alone identifies traits to investigate.

slides.title: Functionalism relates traits to their biological roles
body: **Functionalism** asks what a trait accomplishes for the organism. A limb used for grasping and a limb used for flight perform different tasks even when they share an evolutionary origin.
An action can be described through both its outcome and the processes producing it. Feeding obtains food; sensory detection and motor activity determine how the animal captures or collects it.

The vampire squid’s arms and fine filaments provide recognizable structures for such questions. Researchers can observe what the animal does with them and then investigate the cells and signals controlling their use.

slides.title: Hunting begins with coordinated eye and tail movements
body: A hunting zebrafish turns its eyes toward a shared frontal region and moves its tail. **Eye convergence** is this inward rotation. A **saccade** is a rapid eye movement.

**Calcium imaging** measures activity-related fluorescence inside cells. Recording it alongside eye and tail movements identifies which neurons become active as the fish begins the hunting sequence.

slides.title: Mutation supplies new inherited variation
body: A **mutation** is a change in genetic information. Mutations can alter proteins, development, or the regulation of cellular processes. They provide one source of inherited variation.
A mutation can have little effect, reduce function, or change a trait in a way that matters under particular conditions. Its consequences depend on what changes and where the gene is used.

Natural selection changes the frequency of variants through differences in survival and reproduction. Mutation produces variation; selection changes its distribution across generations. These are different processes.

slides.title: Primate brains share an evolutionary ancestry
body: **Primates** include monkeys, apes, and humans. Related species share inherited traits, while their anatomy and behavior also differ. Shared ancestry explains why some structures recur across species.
A **phylogeny** represents evolutionary ancestry as branches. Branch points mark the divergence of ancestral populations. Humans occupy one branch among other living primates.
Comparisons can separate a broadly shared ability from a specialization. Researchers can ask which vocal, motor, or learning abilities occur in several primates and which differ among their lineages.

slides.title: Brain mass and neuron number are different measurements
body: Brain mass measures how much tissue an animal has. Neuron number measures how many nerve cells it contains. A larger brain does not necessarily contain a proportionally larger number of cortical neurons.
Species differ in neuron size, spacing, and the proportions of different tissues. These differences change how many cells fit within a given brain mass.
The mammalian comparison therefore uses separate measurements of size and cell number. Explaining a behavioral ability also requires examining what those cells do and how they communicate.

slides.title: Speech classification uses a trained readout
body: Brainoware classified recordings from eight speakers. Japanese /a/ and /e/ vowel sounds were converted into electrical stimulation patterns, which entered the organoid through electrodes.

slides.title: Animal research includes care and ethical oversight
body: Animal research requires appropriate housing, veterinary care, and ethical oversight. A proposed experiment must justify its scientific purpose and describe how the animals will be cared for.
The **three Rs** are replacement, reduction, and refinement. Replacement uses suitable alternatives; reduction avoids unnecessary animal use; refinement improves procedures and care to reduce harm.

The sea-lion footage provides an example of a trained movement in managed care. Researchers also measure feeding and voluntary participation when evaluating cognitive activities. Welfare can be examined through repeated observations of the animal’s behavior.

slides.title: Sea lions learn to control a computer cursor
body: Winship and colleagues trained sea lions to operate EVE, an underwater computer interface. A separate display presented a cursor and targets. Directional buttons controlled cursor movement.
The sea lion contacted buttons with its muzzle. Each direction moved the cursor across the screen. Reaching a target produced a success signal and reinforcement.

Training established the button actions before presenting more complex tasks. The animal learned to watch the cursor, choose an input, and stop or change that input as the cursor approached the target.

slides.title: A success tone becomes a conditioned reinforcer
body: A **conditioned reinforcer** is a signal that gains reinforcing value through pairing with other consequences. During EVE training, a success tone was paired with food and other reinforcements.
Early in training, a trainer could deliver the tone manually. Later, software generated it when the cursor touched a target. The sound marked the successful event immediately.

Food, ice, and trainer encouragement followed successful responses. The tone identified which action had earned reinforcement, helping the animal learn the task even when the trainer did not visibly signal the correct movement.

slides.title: Target-contact latency declines during training

A faster trial can involve a straighter route, better-timed release, or less ineffective input. Recorded button sequences identify which actions occurred while the cursor traveled toward the target.

slides.title: Human research includes consent and privacy
body: **Informed consent** means that a person understands the proposed research and voluntarily agrees to participate. Researchers explain the procedures, likely burdens, and the participant’s right to withdraw.
Privacy protects personal information, including clinical history and brain recordings. Researchers limit who can access identifying data and how those data are stored or shared.

Clinical research may include people with neurological injuries or conditions. Their circumstances affect how procedures are explained and what participation requires. Ethical review evaluates these demands before the study begins.

slides.title: Optogenetics makes selected neurons responsive to light
body: **Optogenetics** places a light-sensitive protein in selected cells. An **ion channel** is a protein pathway through the membrane. Opening the channel allows charged particles called ions to cross.
**Channelrhodopsin-2**, or ChR2, comes from an alga. Its light-absorbing molecule, **retinal**, responds to blue light. The protein opens a channel through which positive ions can move.
Light can then change the firing of selected neurons at a chosen time. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for optogenetics.

slides.title: Ion movement changes a cell’s electrical state
body: An **ion** carries electrical charge. Sodium, potassium, and calcium ions are positive; chloride is negative. Different concentrations occur inside and outside a neuron.

An open channel allows ions to cross the membrane. Concentration differences and electrical forces determine their movement. Moving charge changes the **membrane potential**, the voltage difference across the membrane.

A channel’s **selectivity** determines which ions can pass. Changing the available ions changes the measured current. In optogenetics, light opens the channel, ions move, and the neuron’s voltage changes.

slides.title: Channel opening gives a neural signal its time course
body: **Gating** is the opening or closing of an ion channel. Light-gated channels respond to illumination. Voltage-gated channels respond to the membrane voltage.
A flash can open a channel rapidly, while closing takes longer. The electrical current can therefore continue after the brief flash ends. Opening and closing determine the input’s time course.
A neuron receives many inputs at different times. A longer-lasting current overlaps more of those inputs. Channel timing affects whether their combined effect brings the neuron to firing threshold.

slides.title: Depolarization can trigger an action potential
body: A resting neuron is usually more negative inside than outside. **Depolarization** makes this difference less negative. Inward movement of positive charge can bring the membrane to firing threshold.
An **action potential** is a brief electrical signal that renews itself as it travels along an axon. Voltage-gated channels open in sequence as adjacent membrane regions change voltage.

At a **synapse**, one neuron influences another cell. Many synapses release chemical messengers called **neurotransmitters**. Light-triggered firing can therefore change the activity of cells receiving the stimulated neuron’s outputs.

slides.title: Brief light pulses can make neurons fire

slides.title: Excitation and inhibition shape circuit activity
body: **Excitation** increases a neuron’s tendency to fire. **Inhibition** reduces it. The neuron’s output depends on the combined effects of its incoming signals.
The effect of a channel depends on which ions move through it. ChR2 carries positive ions. **Anion channelrhodopsins** carry negative ions such as chloride.
Optical activation and inhibition let researchers change firing in different directions. They can measure how increasing or decreasing activity changes movement, sensation, or another behavior.

slides.title: Inhibitory signals change the probability of firing
body: Inhibition can move a neuron’s voltage away from firing threshold. It can also reduce the effect of an excitatory input by opening another pathway for charge to cross the membrane.

Chloride movement depends on its concentration and the membrane voltage. Opening a chloride channel drives the voltage toward the **chloride equilibrium potential**, where the forces on chloride balance.

Govorunova and colleagues used a light-sensitive chloride channel to suppress firing. Spikes stopped during illumination and resumed afterward. Light controlled the periods in which the neuron sent fewer electrical signals.

slides.title: Activating fly neurons recruits specific actions
body: Inagaki and colleagues used **ReaChR**, a channel activated by longer-wavelength light than ChR2. They placed it in selected fly neurons, allowing red light to change those cells’ activity.
Activating sugar-sensing **Gr5a neurons** triggered extension of the **proboscis**, the fly’s feeding structure. The mouthpart moved outward during illumination.

Other targeted cells produced other actions. Selecting the neuron group determines which response light can recruit. The feeding example makes the sequence concrete: activate sensory neurons, then measure the mouthpart movement.

slides.title: Experience changes how a fly circuit influences courtship
body: **P1 neurons** participate in male fly courtship. Inagaki and colleagues activated them with light and measured courtship actions, including wing extension.
The response differed with the fly’s previous social experience. The same targeted activation could produce different behavior after different housing histories.

slides.title: Wireless optical stimulation delivers pulsed energy
body: A light-emitting device uses electrical energy and produces heat. Montgomery and colleagues measured its light pulses and the temperature changes around it.
**Duty cycle** is the fraction of time the light is on. Short pulses leave more time with the emitter off. Increasing duty cycle increases the average energy delivered.
At 20 mW/mm² and duty cycles up to 20%, the measured temperature rise stayed below 1 °C. Pulse timing therefore changes both neural stimulation and the energy deposited near the tissue.

body: **Neural telemetry** sends recorded brain signals to a remote receiver. Szuts and colleagues placed electrodes and an amplifier on a rat, with a radio transmitter carried in a harness.

slides.title: Wireless recordings follow brain activity during bat flight

Different cells were active in different parts of the route. Their combined activity described spatial position while the bat moved through a three-dimensional environment.

Spatial experience therefore affected activity after the bat stopped flying. The hippocampus organized route-related sequences during both active navigation and subsequent rest.

slides.title: Body landmarks make movement measurable
body: An **anatomical landmark** is a recognizable body feature used for measurement. Snout position describes head movement; wrist and digit positions describe a reach. Each landmark measures a particular part of an action.
A researcher marks the landmark in selected video frames. A trained computer system then locates it in more frames, producing a record of its changing position.

slides.title: Neurons communicate through branching processes
body: A neuron has a cell body and branching **processes**. **Dendrites** receive many incoming signals. An **axon** carries outgoing electrical activity toward other cells.
At a chemical synapse, the sending cell releases a neurotransmitter. The transmitter binds to **receptors**, proteins on the receiving cell, and changes that cell’s response.

Neuronal processes extend across the electrode array. An electrode records voltage changes nearby. Stimulation at one location can affect cells elsewhere as activity travels through the living network.

slides.title: Place and rate codes convey the virtual ball position
body: DishBrain converted the virtual ball’s position into electrical pulses. Eight sensory electrodes delivered inputs. A **place code** uses the location of stimulation to represent a variable.
A **rate code** uses how often pulses occur. The refined protocol used rates from 4 to 40 Hz, giving the culture additional information about the ball.

The neurons received timed electrical pulses rather than seeing a screen. Changing the encoding changed the information available for paddle control. Performance improved across the refined input designs.

slides.title: An action determines the next input in a closed loop
body: **Feedback** means that an action’s result changes what happens next. During navigation, movement changes the visual scene. The new scene then guides another movement.
In DishBrain, the neurons move the paddle. Whether the ball is hit determines the electrical signal sent back to them. Their activity changes the next input they receive.

A **closed loop** repeats this cycle of output and input. In the virtual-aquarium example, a fish’s movement changes the displayed scene. In the culture, neural output changes the game and its subsequent stimulation.

slides.title: Motor-region activity determines paddle movement
body: DishBrain assigned two electrode groups to paddle movement. Activity in one moved the paddle up; activity in the other moved it down.
These **motor regions** were software-defined areas of the array, not an anatomical motor cortex. The computer compared their recorded activity to choose the paddle’s movement.

A hit required appropriately timed movement toward the ball. Spiking somewhere in the culture was not sufficient for effective control. The balance of activity in the assigned regions determined the action.

body: Stowers and colleagues measured an animal’s position and used it to update a virtual scene. Moving through the arena changed the visual input delivered on surrounding displays.
Flies produce an **optomotor response**, turning in response to moving visual patterns. Rotating the virtual scene recruited this response and influenced free-flight direction.

body: A **portal** was a region that changed the displayed world when a zebrafish entered it. The fish stayed in the same tank while the visual scene switched.

slides.title: Freely moving mice avoid virtual depth
body: Stowers and colleagues placed mice on a platform above apparent shallow and deep spaces. Real surfaces were 20 and 40 centimetres below the track. Virtual scenes reproduced these views.
**Motion parallax** is the change in an object’s apparent position as the observer moves. Near and far objects shift differently. Head tracking allowed the displays to reproduce these differences.

Mice preferred the shallow side with real surfaces and perspective-correct virtual scenes. A static display lacked the same preference. Movement-dependent visual changes helped guide where the mice walked.

items.text: Sensory inputs change neuronal activity, and motor outputs produce actions; internal state and prior experience alter the response.

items.lead: Plasticity changes what circuits can do
items.text: Development, practice, and recovery after early injury alter neural organization and the skills remaining tissue can perform.

items.lead: Mechanism and function answer different questions
items.text: Mechanism explains the cells and signals producing an action; function describes what the action accomplishes.

items.lead: Learning depends on consequences and feedback
items.text: Rewarded actions become more effective, while a closed loop makes the next input depend on the system’s own output.
Recording measures activity during behavior; optogenetic activation or inhibition changes selected cells so the resulting behavior can be measured.

items.lead: Biological interfaces require defined inputs and outputs
items.text: A fish controls wheels, a sea lion controls a cursor, and cultured neurons control a paddle through explicit mappings that researchers can test.
